Convex optimization (infz∈C​f(z))

 Home Mathematics Area of mathematics Mathematical optimization
OurBigBook.com Words: 10k Articles: 121
Convex optimization is a minimization problem with a convex function as its objective function and a convex set of feasible points. For a finite-valued f:C→R, the problem is to find z∗​∈C with f(z∗​)≤f(z) for every z∈C. The displayed infimum describes its value even when no minimizing point exists. The two convexity requirements concern different objects: the allowed decisions and the scores assigned to them.
A convex set contains the whole line segment between any two of its points:
u,v∈C,0≤t≤1⟹(1−t)u+tv∈C.
(1)
A convex function lies below the interpolation of its endpoint values:
f((1−t)u+tv)≤(1−t)f(u)+tf(v).
(2)
Thus mixing two allowed decisions preserves feasibility, and the mixed score is no worse than the same mixture of endpoint scores. The objective function may have flat regions or corners. For a strictly convex function, the second inequality is strict when u=v and 0<t<1.
A useful constraint representation is
infz​f(z)subject togi​(z)≤0 (i=1,…,m),Az=b,
(3)
where f,gi​ are convex functions on a common convex set D, and the equalities are affine functions. Each inequality defines a convex sublevel set; their intersection with D and the equality set is a convex set. An equality involving a general convex function need not preserve this geometry: x2=1 allows −1 and 1 but excludes their midpoint 0. See Boyd and Vandenberghe, Convex Optimization (2004), §4.2.1 for the standard problem form.
Why local information can certify a global answer. Every local minimum of a convex optimization problem is a global minimum, including minima on the boundary. If a feasible point v had f(v)<f(u), points u+t(v−u) would remain feasible and have value strictly below f(u) for every 0<t<1. Taking t arbitrarily small contradicts a local minimum at u. This argument explains the special power of convexity: a better distant decision would reveal an improving direction immediately nearby.
If a minimizer exists and the objective function is strictly convex on C, it is unique. Two distinct minimizers of value p∗​ would have a feasible midpoint with value strictly below p∗​. Existence is a separate question: the exponential function ex is strictly convex on R, but its infimum 0 is approached only as x→−∞. Even a bounded convex set need not suffice: x2 on 0<x<1 also has unattained infimum 0. A continuous function on a nonempty compact set attains its minimum by the extreme value theorem.
Nor does strict convexity imply differentiability. For f(x)=x2+∣x∣, the squared term gives the strict inequality while the triangle inequality gives the weak inequality for the absolute value. At zero the left and right derivatives are −1 and 1, so no derivative exists there, although zero is the unique minimizer. Such objectives require subgradients or proximal operators rather than an ordinary gradient at every point.
For a differentiable convex function on an open convex set containing C, the constrained first-order condition is
∇f(z∗​)T(z−z∗​)≥0for every z∈C.
(4)
Indeed, the subgradient inequality f(z)≥f(z∗​)+∇f(z∗​)T(z−z∗​) makes this sufficient; taking the one-sided derivative along feasible line segments makes it necessary. At an interior minimizer, both directions are feasible and the gradient must vanish. At a boundary minimizer it can be nonzero: it only needs to make every feasible direction nondecreasing. See Boyd and Vandenberghe, §§3.1.3 and 4.2.3.
A fully computed nearest-point problem. Project a=(2,1) onto the half-space C={(x,y):x+y≤1} by minimizing half the squared Euclidean distance:
f(x,y)=21​((x−2)2+(y−1)2),g(x,y)=x+y−1≤0.
(5)
The Hessian matrix is the identity matrix, so the objective function is strictly convex. The unconstrained minimizer (2,1) violates the inequality. With the convention g≤0, the optimization Lagrangian is L=f+λg, where the Lagrange multiplier satisfies λ≥0. Its Karush-Kuhn-Tucker conditions are
x+y−1≤0,λ≥0,λ(x+y−1)=0,x−2+λ=0,y−1+λ=0.
(6)
The last two equations give x=2−λ, y=1−λ. The choice λ=0 is infeasible, so complementary slackness forces x+y=1. Consequently 3−2λ=1, giving λ=1, (x∗​,y∗​)=(1,0) and f(x∗​,y∗​)=1. The Euclidean distance is 2​, rather than the objective function value 1. The gradient (−1,−1) at the answer balances λ∇g=(1,1); the displacement from (1,0) to (2,1) is a normal vector to the boundary.
There is an exact certificate independent of numerical search. Completing squares gives
L(x,y,1)=1+21​((x−1)2+y2)≥1.
(7)
For every feasible point, g≤0 implies L(x,y,1)≤f(x,y). Thus every feasible objective is at least 1, and (1,0) attains this bound. More generally the Lagrangian dual problem has objective q(λ)=infx,y​L(x,y,λ)=2λ−λ2=1−(λ−1)2 for λ≥0. Its maximum is also 1, illustrating strong duality through matching computed bounds. This makes the example a model for Euclidean projection onto a convex set and the projection step in projected gradient descent.
What the multiplier conditions require. For differentiable convex functions f,gi​ on an open convex set D and equalities Az=b defined by affine functions, the KKT conditions combine feasibility, λi​≥0, complementary slackness λi​gi​(z∗​)=0, and stationarity
∇f(z∗​)+∑i​λi​∇gi​(z∗​)+ATν=0,
(8)
with unrestricted equality Lagrange multipliers ν. They suffice to certify a global minimum without an additional regularity assumption: the optimization Lagrangian is convex, stationarity minimizes it, and feasibility with complementary slackness gives the same certificate as above. To guarantee their necessity at an attained finite optimum, a regularity hypothesis suffices: Slater's condition requires some zˉ∈D with gi​(zˉ)<0 and Azˉ=b. The projection example has the strictly feasible point (0,0). See Boyd and Vandenberghe, §§5.2.3 and 5.5.3. This hypothesis guarantees suitable multipliers, not existence of a primal minimizer.
Without regularity, necessity can fail even for convex functions: minimize f(x)=x subject to g(x)=x2≤0. The sole feasible point x=0 is optimal, but stationarity would require 1+λ⋅0=0. No Lagrange multiplier works. There is no strictly feasible point, and the gradient of the constraint vanishes at the answer.
The nonconvex contrast. The polynomial h(x)=(x2−1)2+0.2x has derivative h′(x)=4x3−4x+0.2 and second derivative h′′(x)=12x2−4. Numerically solving the cubic gives stationary points −1.024120300, 0.050125947, and 0.973994353. Their objective values are respectively −0.202440434, 1.005006281, and 0.197434153, with second derivatives 8.585869, −3.969849, and 7.383980. Hence both outer points are local minima, and the middle point is a local maximum. Since h(x)→+∞ at both ends, its global minimum exists and must be one of the stationary minima: it is the left one. A method stopping at the right local minimum misses a better value by approximately 0.399874587.
The practical appeal of convex optimization is the ability to check an answer globally using geometry and matching Lagrangian duality bounds. The projection certificate certifies every feasible alternative at once; the tilted quartic shows why a zero gradient alone cannot do that for general nonlinear optimization.
Historically, an early landmark is Kuhn and Tucker's [ref]. Its §3 explicitly states a regularity hypothesis for inequality-constrained Lagrange multipliers; its discussion of saddle points explains how concave functions support global conclusions for maximization. This documents an early formulation of the multiplier approach; it does not establish sole discovery of today's KKT conditions or of convex optimization as a whole.

Pari-mutuel expected-return allocation (xi​=(pi​si​/τ​−si​)+)

Words: 76
Convex optimization OurBigBook.com
For positive existing stakes si​ and budget b, maximizing ∑i​pi​xi​/(si​+xi​) is equivalent to minimizing ∑i​pi​si​/(si​+xi​). A positive multiplier τ chosen so that ∑i​xi​=b gives the displayed allocation. Each coordinate minimizes pi​si​/(si​+x)+τx on x≥0, which proves global optimality by Lagrangian sufficiency theorem. Its active set is ordered by pi​/si​. Zero existing stakes require a separate payoff convention and can cause nonattainment; the positive-stake formula should not be extended through undefined ratios.

Separation oracle

Words: 112 Articles: 1
Convex optimization OurBigBook.com
A separation oracle either certifies that a supplied point belongs to a convex feasible set or returns a violated linear inequality whose half-space contains the whole feasible set. Its running time can be small even when the set has exponentially many defining inequalities. Together with rational encoding bounds and an outer bound, this permits polynomial time ellipsoid method feasibility and optimization.

Path-constraint separation by shortest paths (∑e∈p​xe​≥1(p:s⇝t))

Words: 57
Separation oracle OurBigBook.com
After testing nonnegative edge coordinates and any explicit box or budget inequalities, treat those coordinates as lengths. A shortest path of length below one supplies a violated path inequality; a minimum length at least one certifies all path inequalities. If no source-to-target path exists, all those inequalities are vacuous. Thus a polynomial time shortest path problem calculation separates an exponentially constrained linear program.

Chambolle–Pock algorithm

Words: 126 Articles: 1
Convex optimization OurBigBook.com
For a saddle point problem minu​maxv​{F(u)+⟨Du,v⟩−G(v)}, one update ordering is
uk+1=proxτF​(uk−τD∗vk),vk+1=proxσG​(vk+σD(2uk+1−uk)).
(9)
The proximal operators treat both nonsmooth convex terms, while the extrapolation 2uk+1−uk couples the primal and dual variables. The primal objective is F(u)+G∗(Du), with G∗ the convex conjugate. A dual-first ordering is obtained by exchanging roles; consistent indexing is needed when comparing the formulas.

Convergence of primal-dual hybrid gradient (τσ∥D∥2<1)

Words: 68
Chambolle–Pock algorithm OurBigBook.com
For proper lower semicontinuous convex functions on finite-dimensional Hilbert spaces, a nonempty saddle point set, and constant positive steps satisfying the displayed inequality, the primal-dual hybrid gradient method with extrapolation parameter one converges to a saddle point. The strict condition controls the bilinear coupling by the operator norm. It does not remove the need for existence of a saddle point. The fixed-step theorem and assumptions are recalled in Malitsky and Pock, A first-order primal-dual algorithm with linesearch, Section 1.

Convex positively one-homogeneous functional (J(tu)=tJ(u)(t≥0))

Words: 198 Articles: 1
Convex optimization OurBigBook.com
This is a proper convex function that has degree-one positive homogeneity, with J(0)=0. It need not be even or nonnegative; linear functionals are examples. Its subdifferential satisfies
p∈∂J(u)⟺⟨p,u⟩=J(u) and ⟨p,z⟩≤J(z) for every z.
(10)
The two tests z=0 and z=2u prove equality; the subgradient inequality then gives the global upper bound. Conversely that bound and equality prove the subgradient condition. Hence a subgradient at u also supports every nonnegative multiple of u. Requiring J(−u)=J(u) gives an absolutely one-homogeneous functional.

Generalized eigenfunction in the forward-operator metric (λK∗Ku∈∂J(u))

Words: 123
Convex positively one-homogeneous functional OurBigBook.com
A nonzero u satisfying this relation, with Ku=0, generalizes the eigenfunction of an absolutely one-homogeneous functional to the quadratic geometry induced by the forward map. Pairing with u yields λ=J(u)/∥Ku∥2. With unit data norm it is a generalized singular vector. If λ>0, 0≤αλ≤1 and the exact data are Ku, the vector (1−αλ)u minimizes the quadratic variational regularization objective. Substitute its raywise subgradient into the subgradient optimality condition. Every minimizing branch has the same predicted data, and injectivity of K gives equality of vectors. The Bregman distance along this ray is zero even though the reconstruction is shrunk. For nonnegative J the branch continues as (1−αλ)+​u; nonnegativity supplies 0∈∂J(0) for the threshold argument.
Background on these generalized singular vectors: Benning and Burger, Ground States and Singular Vectors of Convex Variational Regularization Methods.

Conic optimization

Words: 3k Articles: 21
Convex optimization OurBigBook.com
Optimization of a linear function subject to affine constraints and membership in a closed convex cone. Choosing the positive semidefinite cone gives semidefinite programming; other choices include copositive optimization and completely positive optimization. Dual cones produce scalar-product bounds on feasible objectives.

Farkas' lemma (Az=b, z≥0orATy≥0, bTy<0)

Words: 1k Articles: 3
Conic optimization OurBigBook.com
For a real matrix A∈Rm×n and a vector b∈Rm, exactly one of the following systems has a solution:
​Az=b,z∈Rn,z≥0;ATy≥0,y∈Rm,bTy<0.​
(11)
The linear inequalities here are componentwise. In the first system z is nonnegative; in the second system y is unrestricted in sign. The second system is a certificate that the first has no feasible point. This nonnegative-equations alternative is developed in Boyd and Vandenberghe, Convex Optimization slides, §5.34.
Build the target, or separate it. Write the columns of A as a1​,…,an​. Then Az=∑j​zj​aj​ is a conic combination: its coefficients must be nonnegative, but need not sum to one. The obtainable targets form the finitely generated cone
K={Az:z≥0}=cone{a1​,…,an​}.
(12)
A solution z explains how to build b from those columns. A certificate y instead defines a linear functional v↦yTv. The condition ATy≥0 says that its dot product with every generating column is nonnegative, and hence with every point of K. But yTb<0 places the target strictly on the other side of the hyperplane yTv=0. Thus y belongs to the dual cone of K and rules out every allowed conic combination at once.
A certificate that can be checked by eye. Take the identity matrix
A=I2​=(10​01​),b=(−11​).
(13)
Here K is the nonnegative orthant. The equation Az=b forces z=(−1,1)T, violating z≥0. The certificate y=(1,0)T gives
ATy=(10​)≥0,bTy=−1<0.
(14)
The linear functional simply reads the first coordinate: all allowed column combinations have a nonnegative first coordinate, while b has first coordinate −1. For comparison, the target (1,1)T is obtained with z=(1,1)T.
Why this is useful and striking. A successful search can exhibit one feasible point; an unsuccessful search alone cannot explain why every candidate fails. Farkas' lemma guarantees an equally concrete witness of impossibility for this finite linear problem. Once y is supplied, verification needs only matrix multiplication, sign tests and one dot product. The same idea gives a Farkas certificate for linear inequalities and underlies linear programming duality.
Brief geometric proof. The two systems cannot both hold, because they would imply
0>bTy=(Az)Ty=zT(ATy)≥0.
(15)
For existence of a certificate when b∈/K, closedness of finitely generated cones makes K a closed convex cone, so separation from a closed convex cone supplies yTb<0 and yTv≥0 for every v∈K. Testing each column gives ATy≥0. Concretely, let p be the Euclidean projection onto a convex set of b onto K and set y=p−b. The projection inequality gives yT(v−p)≥0 for v∈K. Testing v=0 and v=2p gives yTp=0, whence yTb=−∥p−b∥22​<0. In the example, p=(0,1)T and y=(1,0)T. Alternatively, the Fenchel-Moreau theorem applied to the cone's indicator functional proves the same separation through its polar cone.
An original historical source is Julius Farkas's [ref]. The linked archival record verifies the author, title and publication details.

Farkas certificate for linear inequalities (CTy=0,y≥0,dTy<0)

Words: 737 Articles: 1
Farkas' lemma OurBigBook.com
Let C∈Rm×n and d∈Rm. For unrestricted x∈Rn, the system of linear inequalities Cx≤d has no feasible point if and only if there is a vector y∈Rm with
y≥0,CTy=0,dTy<0.
(16)
The entries yi​ are nonnegative Lagrange multipliers for the rows. Multiplying inequalities by them preserves their direction; the condition CTy=0 cancels every variable, leaving the contradiction
0=(CTy)Tx=yTCx≤yTd<0.
(17)
This is a Farkas' lemma alternative for non-strict inequalities; no strict-feasibility assumption is needed. See Boyd and Vandenberghe, Convex Optimization (2004), §5.8.3, pp. 261–262.
Three individually possible requirements, jointly impossible. Suppose two unrestricted real coordinates x1​,x2​, drawn as x,y in the diagram, must satisfy
x1​≥1,x2​≥1,x1​+x2​≤1.
(18)
Write every row in the same ≤ direction:
C=​−101​0−11​​,d=​−1−11​​,y=​111​​.
(19)
Then CTy=(0,0)T and dTy=−1. The nonnegative weighted sum, with Lagrange multipliers (1,1,1), is visibly
≤−1−x1​​​+≤−1−x2​​​+≤1(x1​+x2​)​​⟹0≤−1.
(20)
Each individual requirement defines a half-space in the plane. Even every pair has a feasible point: (1,1) satisfies the first two, (1,0) the first and third, and (0,1) the second and third. Their common intersection is empty, because the first two force x1​+x2​≥2, while the third demands at most 1.
Why cancellation is necessary for unrestricted variables. A nonzero linear functional (CTy)Tx can be made arbitrarily positive or negative by varying unrestricted x, so CTy≥0 alone would not yield a contradiction. Equality is essential here. If x≥0 is also imposed, the sufficient certificate becomes y≥0, CTy≥0, dTy<0, because then yTCx≥0. This is the sign convention used in robust infeasibility under uniform constraint relaxation. One can instead append the rows −xj​≤0 and use the equality certificate on the enlarged system. Reversing all constraints to Cx≥d reverses the scalar sign to dTy>0, as in the normalized integer Farkas infeasibility gap.
Checking a solver's infeasibility claim. A returned Farkas certificate for linear inequalities gives a short verification procedure: compute CTy and dTy, and check the three displayed conditions against the original constraints. Any positive multiple is another certificate; division by −dTy normalizes dTy to −1. With rational numbers as data and certificate, the tests can be exact. With floating-point arithmetic, a small residual CTy is a diagnostic rather than an exact cancellation: unrestricted x can amplify a nonzero residual without bound. A rigorous certificate therefore needs exact cancellation or justified error bounds and additional bounds on the variables. The strict negative scalar is the margin of contradiction.
The same weighted sums give dual bounds. For the linear program maximizing cTx over unrestricted x with Cx≤d, any y≥0 satisfying CTy=c gives
cTx=yTCx≤yTd
(21)
for every feasible point. Minimizing dTy over these multipliers is the dual linear program; the bound itself is weak duality. For example, maximize x1​+x2​ subject to −x1​≤0, −x2​≤0, x1​+x2​≤1. The multipliers (0,0,1) give the upper bound 1, attained at (1,0). The infeasibility example above uses the same row directions, but lower bounds of 1 on both coordinates. Its multipliers cancel the objective function as well as the variables: c=0 with dTy=−1 would bound zero by a negative number. Thus impossibility and linear programming optimality certificates use the same arithmetic. See Boyd and Vandenberghe, Convex Optimization slides, §§5.32–5.35 for infeasibility as a dual alternative.
Why every inconsistent system has such a certificate. Introduce a slack variable vector s≥0 and write Cx+s=d. Split the unrestricted vector as x=u−v with u,v≥0. Applying Farkas' lemma to the column matrix [C −C Im​] gives CTy≥0, −CTy≥0, y≥0 and dTy<0. The first two conditions together are exactly CTy=0. This reduction explains both the equality and the nonnegative row multipliers.
Normalized integer Farkas infeasibility gap (bTλ≥[(n+1)U]−(n+1))
Words: 130
Farkas certificate for linear inequalities OurBigBook.com
Suppose A,b have integer entries of absolute value at most U≥1, A has n columns, and Ax≥b is infeasible. A Farkas certificate for linear inequalities can be chosen with λ≥0, ATλ=0, 1Tλ=1 and the displayed lower bound. Normalize an infeasibility certificate to obtain the last equality, then maximize bTλ over the resulting compact linear polyhedron. A maximizing extreme point has at most n+1 positive entries: otherwise the augmented columns (AiT​,1) on its support would be dependent, allowing feasible perturbations in both directions. For its k≤n+1 independent supported columns, select k independent equations. Cramer's rule expresses the supported entries with a common nonzero integer determinant denominator. That determinant has absolute value at most k!Uk≤[(n+1)U]n+1. The positive value bTλ therefore has a positive integer numerator over a denominator of at most this size, proving the bound.

Interior-point method

Words: 553 Articles: 8
Conic optimization OurBigBook.com
An interior-point method solves constrained mathematical optimization problems by maintaining variables in the interiors of their feasible cones or inequality domains. Barrier derivatives are defined there, and damped Newton methods keep subsequent iterates in their domains. A central path gives a family of barrier-regularized optima whose duality gap approaches zero; a conic phase-I problem can supply a strict feasible starting point.

Taking K=R+m​ gives componentwise linear inequalities; taking a second-order cone gives a Euclidean norm constraint. A self-dual cone has K∗=K, but this equality does not guarantee a feasible point or strong duality.

Infimal convolution (E□F)

Convex analysis OurBigBook.com
An infimal convolution is the cheapest way to split a prescribed total between two costs. Suppose two activities contribute u and v to a required total x, costing f(u) and g(v). Their combined cost is optimized over all splits u+v=x, rather than charging both activities for the entire total.
For proper extended-real functions f,g:X→R∪{+∞} on a real vector space X, define
h(x)=(f□g)(x)=infu∈X​{f(u)+g(x−u)}=infu+v=x​{f(u)+g(v)}.
(40)
The definition does not require convexity. An infinite cost forbids that contribution, as with an indicator functional of a constraint set. If no split has two finite costs, set h(x)=+∞; if the costs of admissible splits are unbounded below, h(x)=−∞. Thus proper inputs need not produce a proper extended-real function. The notation E□F denotes the same operation. See Parikh and Boyd, Proximal Algorithms, §3.1 for the standard convex analysis definition and its connection to the Moreau envelope.
An infimum is a best lower bound, whereas a minimum is a value realized by some split. Writing min in place of inf requires an attaining pair (u∗​,v∗​). For convex functions, mixing two nearly optimal splits and applying convexity to each cost proves that their infimal convolution is convex whenever it is proper; one must use nearly optimal splits because exact minimizers need not exist. Its convex conjugate is f∗+g∗ whenever the extended real number arithmetic is well defined; see conjugate of an infimal convolution for the precise identity. This turns the optimization over splits into addition in the conjugate variables.
Two quadratic costs: share the load according to its price. Let X=R and let the convex quadratic functions be
f(u)=2a​u2,g(v)=2b​v2,a,b>0.
(41)
For fixed x, eliminate v=x−u. The derivative of the total cost is au−b(x−u), so equal marginal costs give
u∗​=a+bb​x,v∗​=a+ba​x,au∗​=bv∗​.
(42)
The cheaper activity receives more of a positive total: when a<b and x>0, u∗​>v∗​. Completing the square gives an exact certificate for every competing split:
2a​u2+2b​(x−u)2=2(a+b)ab​x2+2a+b​(u−a+bb​x)2.
(43)
Consequently the infimum is a unique minimum, and
(f□g)(x)=21​a+bab​x2.
(44)
The effective quadratic coefficient is c=ab/(a+b), with 1/c=1/a+1/b. It is smaller than either a or b: allowing both activities reduces the cost compared with assigning everything to either one. If a=b, each receives half the total and c=a/2. This is a simple quadratic optimization problem whose answer preserves the form of the original costs.
Smoothing a corner by splitting its cost. Take the absolute value function f(u)=∣u∣ and the convex quadratic function g(v)=v2/(2t), with t>0. This infimal convolution is the Moreau envelope of the absolute value function:
u∗​=sgn(x)max(∣x∣−t,0),v∗​=x−u∗​,(f□g)(x)={x2/(2t),∣x∣−t/2,​∣x∣≤t,∣x∣>t.​
(45)
Here sgn is the sign function, with sgn(0)=0. The optimal u∗​ is soft thresholding. In the central region, the quadratic function carries the whole total; outside it, v∗​ stays at tsgn(x) and the absolute value function carries the excess. At t=1 the result is the Huber loss in the normalization x2/2 near zero and ∣x∣−1/2 outside. Its derivative is x for ∣x∣≤1 and sgn(x) outside, so the corner becomes a continuous change of slope. Parikh and Boyd's [ref] uses twice this normalization for the Huber loss; the explicit formula here fixes the convention. This is also the one-dimensional case of the existing Moreau envelope of the Euclidean norm.

Finite-valued infimal convolution

Words: 392 Articles: 1
Infimal convolution OurBigBook.com
If two nonnegative finite-valued convex functions are defined on all of a finite-dimensional space, their infimal convolution is finite, convex and continuous everywhere. Convex perturbation duality then gives strong duality and dual attainment at every argument. It does not require or imply attainment of the primal decomposition infimum.
More precisely, let f,g:Rn→[0,∞) be finite everywhere and write h=f□g. Nonnegativity supplies a lower bound, while the two trial splits (x,0) and (0,x) give
0≤h(x)≤min{f(x)+g(0), f(0)+g(x)}<∞.
(46)
Mixing nearly optimal splits proves convexity, and continuity of a convex function applies because the effective domain is the entire finite-dimensional vector space. These statements concern the optimized value, rather than existence of an optimal split. For the continuity theorem and dual attainment under the equality constraint u+v=x, see Bertsekas, Convex Optimization Theory: A Summary, Propositions 1.3.11 and 5.3.3(a). The equality has a feasible point in the whole space for every x, and the displayed bound makes its optimal value finite.
A finite value without any optimal split. On R, take the convex functions f(u)=eu and g(v)=0. Both are nonnegative and finite everywhere, but
(f□g)(x)=infu∈R​eu=0
(47)
for every x. The splits (u,v)=(−k,x+k) have costs e−k→0, yet the exponential function is strictly positive at every finite u. No split attains the infimum. The value function is even constant and differentiable; regularity of the value function does not prevent optimizing splits from escaping to infinity. For example, k=1,3,6 gives costs approximately 0.367879, 0.049787 and 0.002479.
A sufficient extra condition for attainment at a fixed x is that u↦f(u)+g(x−u) be a coercive function, meaning it tends to +∞ as ∥u∥→∞. Under the finite-valued assumptions it is a continuous function, so a sufficiently large closed ball contains a global minimum by the extreme value theorem. If this cost is also a strictly convex function, the optimal split is unique. The quadratic example above satisfies both conditions; the exponential function example does not satisfy coercivity.
Nonnegativity is sufficient, not necessary: finite lower bounds f≥A, g≥B would give h≥A+B by the same argument. Removing all lower-bound control can lose finiteness even for finite convex functions: f(u)=u and g(v)=−v give f(u)+g(x−u)=2u−x, hence h(x)=−∞. Nor does finiteness alone guarantee differentiability: choosing f=g=∣⋅∣ gives h(x)=∣x∣ by the triangle inequality and the split (x,0).

where p⋅x is the dot product and domf={x:f(x)<+∞} is the effective domain. An infinite value of f excludes that input from the supremum. The value f∗(p) can be +∞, but cannot be −∞ because an input with finite f(x) supplies a finite lower bound.
The convex conjugate is automatically a convex function, even when f is not convex: each fixed input gives an affine function p↦p⋅x−f(x), and their supremum is convex. It is also lower semicontinuous. It need not be proper: for f(x)=−x2 on R, px−f(x)=px+x2 is unbounded above for every p. The definition and the automatic convexity are discussed in Boyd and Vandenberghe, Convex Optimization (2004), §3.3.1.
The best lower bound with a prescribed slope. Whenever f∗(p) is finite, the affine function
ℓp​(x)=p⋅x−f∗(p)
(50)
is an affine minorant of f. Indeed, an affine function p⋅x+b lies below f everywhere exactly when b≤infx​(f(x)−p⋅x)=−f∗(p). Thus −f∗(p) is the largest possible intercept at slope p. The convex conjugate trades positions for slopes: x specifies where to inspect f, whereas p specifies which global affine minorant to use. Taking the supremum over all these affine minorants produces the biconjugate; the Fenchel-Moreau theorem says this recovers a proper convex function when it is lower semicontinuous.
A quadratic, computed by completing the square. For the convex quadratic function f(x)=x2/2,
px−2x2​=2p2​−2(x−p)2​.
(51)
Consequently f∗(p)=p2/2, and the unique maximizing input is x=p. The affine minorant ℓp​(x)=px−p2/2 is the tangent line at (p,p2/2): its slope is p and its intercept is −f∗(p)=−p2/2. For example, p=2 gives f∗(2)=2 and the tangent line 2x−2, touching at (2,2). This is the same curve described either by its point values or by the intercepts of its tangent lines.
A corner turns into a constraint on slopes. For the absolute value f(x)=∣x∣, if ∣p∣≤1 then px−∣x∣≤0, with value zero at x=0. If p>1, taking x→+∞ makes (p−1)x→+∞; if p<−1, taking x→−∞ does the same. Therefore its convex conjugate is zero on [−1,1] and +∞ outside: it is the indicator functional of a constraint set for this interval. For ∣p∣<1 the unique maximizing input is zero; for p=1 every x≥0 maximizes, and for p=−1 every x≤0 maximizes. The corner's many supporting slopes are exactly the subdifferential ∂f(0)=[−1,1].
A supremum need not be attained. For a differentiable convex function finite on all of Rn, an input maximizes p⋅x−f(x) exactly when p=∇f(x). If f is strictly convex, there is at most one such input; existence is a separate issue. For the exponential function f(x)=ex, the derivative is positive. At p>0, solving p=ex gives x=logp and f∗(p)=plogp−p. At p=0, the supremum of −ex is zero as x→−∞, with no maximizing input. At p<0, px−ex→+∞ as x→−∞. Thus a strictly convex differentiable function can have both unattained finite conjugate values and infinite conjugate values.

Geometric separation of its epigraph turns containing closed half-spaces into affine lower bounds. Vertical half-spaces are recovered by adding multiples of a domain-separating inequality to one fixed affine minorant.

Fenchel–Young inequality (f(x)+f∗(p)≥p⋅x)

Words: 585 Articles: 1
Convex conjugate OurBigBook.com
The Fenchel–Young inequality says that every input and every slope obey
f(x)+f∗(p)≥p⋅x,x,p∈Rn,
(56)
where f is any proper extended-real function and f∗ is its convex conjugate. No convexity assumption on f is needed for this inequality: the defining supremum is at least the particular value p⋅x−f(x). If either term on the left is +∞, the inequality still holds, but cannot be an equality because the dot product on the right is finite.
For a proper convex function, equality is equivalent to the subgradient condition
f(x)+f∗(p)=p⋅x⟺p∈∂f(x).
(57)
To see this, with f(x) finite, equality says that x attains the supremum defining f∗(p), so p⋅z−f(z)≤p⋅x−f(x) for every z. Rearranging gives the subgradient inequality f(z)≥f(x)+p⋅(z−x). Geometrically, the affine minorant ℓp​(z)=p⋅z−f∗(p) touches f at x.
If the proper convex function is also closed, meaning its epigraph is a closed set, or equivalently it is lower semicontinuous, then
p∈∂f(x)⟺x∈∂f∗(p).
(58)
The forward implication holds without closedness; the reverse one requires the additional hypothesis in general. Applying the equality criterion to f∗ relates x∈∂f∗(p) to f∗∗(x)+f∗(p)=p⋅x, and the Fenchel-Moreau theorem supplies f∗∗=f when f is closed. See Bertsekas, Convex Optimization Theory: A Summary, §5.4.1, Proposition 5.4.3 for precisely this distinction.
A concrete failure of the reverse implication occurs for the indicator functional of a constraint set f of the open interval (−1,1). Its convex conjugate is f∗(p)=∣p∣: the endpoint gives the supremum, even though it is excluded from the interval. At (x,p)=(1,1), x∈∂f∗(p)={1}, but f(1)=+∞, so equality fails and ∂f(1) is empty. Closing the interval changes the endpoint value and restores equality there.
For the convex quadratic function f(x)=x2/2, the Fenchel–Young inequality is x2/2+p2/2≥px, and equality holds exactly when x=p. For the absolute value f(x)=∣x∣, finite equality requires p=sgn(x) at x=0, where sgn is the sign function; at x=0 every p∈[−1,1] gives equality. These are exactly the subgradients of the absolute value, including its entire interval of slopes at the corner.

Fenchel–Young gap (Gf​(x,p)=f(x)+f∗(p)−p⋅x)

Words: 279
Fenchel–Young inequality OurBigBook.com
The Fenchel–Young gap is the nonnegative discrepancy
Gf​(x,p)=f(x)+f∗(p)−p⋅x≥0
(59)
for a proper convex function and its convex conjugate. It can be +∞. When f∗(p) is finite, it is the vertical distance between f(x) and its affine minorant ℓp​(x)=p⋅x−f∗(p). The Fenchel–Young gap vanishes exactly when p∈∂f(x), so it measures whether an input and a slope satisfy the subgradient relation.
For the convex quadratic function f(x)=x2/2, completing the square gives
Gf​(x,p)=2x2​+2p2​−px=2(x−p)2​.
(60)
At x=−1 and p=2, the function value is 1/2 and the tangent line 2x−2 has value −4, giving a Fenchel–Young gap of 9/2. In Rn, the same calculation for f(x)=∥x∥22​/2 gives f∗(p)=∥p∥22​/2 and Gf​(x,p)=∥x−p∥22​/2, half the squared Euclidean norm of the mismatch.
An exact optimization error certificate. Fix a slope p with f∗(p)<+∞ and minimize the linearly tilted objective function hp​(z)=f(z)−p⋅z. By the definition of the convex conjugate, infz​hp​(z)=−f∗(p), so
hp​(x)−infz​hp​(z)=Gf​(x,p).
(61)
This identity holds even when the infimum is not attained. Thus a computed finite Fenchel–Young gap is exactly the error in objective value for this minimization problem. For the convex quadratic function, Gf​(x,p)≤ε implies ∣x−p∣≤2ε​. A general proper convex function need not convert a small gap into a small distance: the absolute value has zero gap at p=1 for every x≥0.
The Fenchel–Young gap also connects convex analysis to optimal transport. For a proper convex function Φ, define Kantorovich potentials u(x)=∥x∥22​/2−Φ(x) and v(y)=∥y∥22​/2−Φ∗(y). The half-squared Euclidean distance cost satisfies ∥x−y∥22​/2−u(x)−v(y)=GΦ​(x,y). For a transport plan with finite integrated cost and integrable Kantorovich potentials, integrating this identity gives the difference between transport cost and the potentials' bound. This is the same local subgradient mismatch summed over transported pairs.

For a jointly smooth convex function f(x,y), update y implicitly by its proximal minimization at fixed x, then update x explicitly with the gradient at the mixed point (x,y+). The combined map is (τL/2)-averaged for 0<τL<2, as follows by applying cocoercivity at two mixed points. Its fixed points are precisely the minimizers. If a minimizer exists, averaged iteration proves convergence.
Implicit nonsmooth block in alternating proximal-gradient iteration
Words: 70
Alternating proximal-gradient operator OurBigBook.com
For f(x,y)=h(x,y)+ϕ(y), where h is convex with an Lh​-Lipschitz gradient and ϕ is convex, use a proximal y-step for the full section and an explicit x-step for h. Monotonicity of the two selected subgradients of ϕ combines with cocoercivity of ∇h to make the full update firmly nonexpansive for 0<τLh​≤1. Existence of a minimizer then gives convergence, even though the full objective is not smooth.
Mixed-point norm identity for alternating updates (∥(p−τa,q)∥2−∥(p,q+τb)∥2)
Words: 53
Alternating proximal-gradient operator OurBigBook.com
For two mixed points with difference (p,q) and gradient difference (a,b), the input difference is (p,q+τb) and the output difference is (p−τa,q). Their squared-norm difference is −2τ(⟨p,a⟩+⟨q,b⟩)+τ2(∥a∥2−∥b∥2). This exact identity is a reusable way to prove averagedness without assuming the two block maps are individually nonexpansive.

Iterative soft-thresholding algorithm

Words: 34
Proximal gradient method OurBigBook.com
The iterative soft-thresholding algorithm applies the proximal gradient method to ∥x∥1​+21​∥Ax−y∥22​:
xk+1=Sτ​(xk−τAT(Axk−y)),0<τ≤∥A∥2→2−2​.
(71)
Here Sτ​ is coordinatewise soft thresholding. The objective is convex and coercive, so iterates converge to a minimizer in finite dimensions; uniqueness requires additional hypotheses.

Subgradient method

Words: 44
Convex optimization OurBigBook.com
The subgradient method minimizes a possibly nonsmooth convex function by choosing gk​∈∂f(xk​) and iterating
xk+1​=xk​−tk​gk​.
(72)
If the subgradients are bounded by G and a minimizer is within distance R of x0​, a suitable constant or diminishing step size finds objective error at most ϵ in O(R2G2/ϵ2) iterations.

Log-sum-exp function (LSEβ​)

Words: 52 Articles: 1
Convex optimization OurBigBook.com
For z∈Rm and β>0, the scaled log-sum-exp function is
LSEβ​(z)=β1​log∑i=1m​eβzi​.
(73)
It is a smooth convex function satisfying
maxi​zi​≤LSEβ​(z)≤maxi​zi​+βlogm​.
(74)

Smooth maximum

Words: 27
Log-sum-exp function OurBigBook.com
Composing the log-sum-exp function with finitely many affine functions gives a differentiable approximation to their pointwise maximum. Increasing the inverse-temperature parameter β reduces the uniform approximation error while increasing the Lipschitz gradient constant.

Nesterov accelerated gradient method

Words: 50
Convex optimization OurBigBook.com
For a convex objective with an L-Lipschitz gradient, Nesterov's accelerated gradient method reaches objective error δ in O(LR2/δ​) iterations when a minimizer lies within distance R of the initial point.
This is an accelerated variant of gradient descent; it should not be identified with every first-order or proximal gradient method.

Monotone operator

Words: 456 Articles: 13
Convex optimization OurBigBook.com
An operator F on an inner product space is monotone when
⟨F(v)−F(w),v−w⟩≥0
(75)
for every v,w. The gradient of every differentiable convex function is monotone.

Cocoercivity (⟨Gz−Gw,z−w⟩≥β∥Gz−Gw∥2)

Words: 80 Articles: 1
Monotone operator OurBigBook.com
An operator G is β-cocoercive when ⟨Gz−Gw,z−w⟩≥β∥Gz−Gw∥2 with β>0. This strengthens monotonicity and implies a Lipschitz constant 1/β by the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality. Gradient maps of smooth convex functions provide an important converse through the Baillon–Haddad theorem.

Baillon–Haddad theorem (⟨∇f(u)−∇f(v),u−v⟩≥L−1∥∇f(u)−∇f(v)∥2)

Words: 45
Cocoercivity OurBigBook.com
On the whole Euclidean space, an L-Lipschitz gradient of a convex function is 1/L-cocoercive. Subtract the supporting affine function at one point, apply the descent lemma to a gradient step at the other point, then interchange the points and add. The conclusion needs convexity but no second derivative.

Resolvent of a monotone operator (JτA​=(I+τA)−1)

Words: 50
Monotone operator OurBigBook.com
For an operator A, its resolvent with step τ>0 is JτA​=(I+τA)−1. A maximal monotone operator has an everywhere-defined single-valued firmly nonexpansive mapping as its resolvent. For A=∂f, the resolvent is the proximal map of τf. This monotone-operator resolvent uses a different convention from the spectral resolvent of a linear operator.

Maximal monotone operator

Words: 35
Monotone operator OurBigBook.com
A monotone operator is maximal when its graph has no proper enlargement that is still monotone. In Euclidean or Hilbert space, its resolvent of a monotone operator is single-valued and everywhere defined for every positive step. Subdifferentials of proper lower semicontinuous convex functions are fundamental examples.

Nonexpansive mapping

Words: 123 Articles: 3
Monotone operator OurBigBook.com
A mapping T on a normed vector space is nonexpansive when ∥T(v)−T(w)∥≤∥v−w∥ for every v,w.

Averaged operator (T=(1−α)I+αR)

Words: 110 Articles: 2
Nonexpansive mapping OurBigBook.com
An operator is α-averaged for 0<α<1 when T=(1−α)I+αR for a nonexpansive mapping R. Averaging controls the update residual and enables fixed-point iteration. A firmly nonexpansive mapping is exactly a 1/2-averaged operator.
Browder convergence theorem for averaged operators
Words: 49
Averaged operator OurBigBook.com
In finite-dimensional Euclidean space, iterating an averaged operator with a nonempty fixed-point set converges in norm to a fixed point from every start. The averaged-operator inequality proves boundedness and a vanishing residual; compactness produces a fixed cluster point and Fejér monotonicity turns subsequential convergence into convergence of the full sequence. A fixed point must exist.
Averaged-operator inequality (∥Tz−Tw∥2≤∥z−w∥2−α1−α​∥(I−T)z−(I−T)w∥2)
Words: 31
Averaged operator OurBigBook.com
The defining averaging representation is equivalent to ∥Tz−Tw∥2≤∥z−w∥2−(1−α)∥(I−T)z−(I−T)w∥2/α. Expanding the norm of the convex combination proves both directions. Substituting a fixed point for w gives Fejér monotonicity and summability of squared residuals.

Firmly nonexpansive mapping

Words: 27
Monotone operator OurBigBook.com
A mapping T on an inner product space is firmly nonexpansive when
∥T(v)−T(w)∥2≤⟨T(v)−T(w),v−w⟩.
(76)
Every firmly nonexpansive mapping is nonexpansive, and the resolvent of a maximal monotone operator is firmly nonexpansive.

Proximal point algorithm

Words: 121 Articles: 3
Monotone operator OurBigBook.com
The proximal point algorithm seeks a zero of a monotone operator F by repeatedly applying its resolvent:
wk+1​=(I+λF)−1wk​.
(77)
For F=∂f, this is iteration of a proximal operator.

Douglas–Rachford method

Words: 68 Articles: 1
Proximal point algorithm OurBigBook.com
For two proximal maps Pf​,Ph​, define reflected maps Rf​=2Pf​−I and Rh​=2Ph​−I. The Douglas--Rachford fixed-point map is
T=21​(I+Rf​Rh​)=I−Ph​+Pf​(2Ph​−I).
(78)
Because reflected proximal maps are nonexpansive, T is firmly nonexpansive.
Product-space reformulation of convex feasibility
Words: 39
Douglas–Rachford method OurBigBook.com
Finding a point in ⋂j=1ℓ​Cj​ is equivalent to intersecting the product C1​×⋯×Cℓ​ with the diagonal subspace in (Rn)ℓ. Projection onto the product is componentwise, while projection onto the diagonal replaces every component by their average.

Preconditioned proximal point algorithm

Words: 26
Proximal point algorithm OurBigBook.com
Given a positive-definite matrix M, the preconditioned proximal point map is
T=(M+F)−1M.
(79)
It is firmly nonexpansive in the weighted inner product ⟨v,w⟩M​=⟨v,Mw⟩ whenever F is monotone.

Primal-dual optimal point

Words: 33
Convex optimization OurBigBook.com
A primal-dual optimal point consists of a feasible solution of an optimization problem and a feasible solution of its Lagrangian dual problem whose objective values agree. Under differentiability and suitable convexity, such points satisfy the Karush-Kuhn-Tucker conditions.

Equality-constrained convex optimization

Words: 34
Convex optimization OurBigBook.com
An equality-constrained convex optimization problem has the form
minx​f(x)subject to Ax=b,
(80)
where f is convex and the constraint is affine. Its stationarity and feasibility equations can be combined into a monotone primal-dual operator.

Proximal gradient methods for learning

Words: 44
Convex optimization OurBigBook.com
These methods optimize a smooth loss plus a term with a tractable proximal operator, such as a sparsity regularizer or a convex-set indicator. The basic proximal gradient method combines a gradient step with a proximal step; projected gradient and accelerated variants are related members of the family.
